look_here_first: LOOK BELOW THE LEAVES: a prostrate rooting mat of alternate, entire, kidney-shaped leaves on thin petioles. Look for tawny silky hairs (especially underneath). Find a tiny PALE, 5-lobed flower and trace its VERY SHORT flower/fruit stalk: the upper end hooks sharply DOWNWARD (recurved), not just a drooping leaf stalk. At maturity compare fruit (3–4 mm) with its persistent five sepals (~2.9–3.8 mm). Larger leaves alone are NOT enough to separate this species from Carolina ponyfoot.

taxonomic_note: Dichondra recurvata Tharp & M.C.Johnst., accepted by Kew POWO/World Flora Online and FNA. FNA reports endemic to Texas; regional published vouchers exist in Hill Country, including Mason and Enchanted Rock. No user-project BONAP county target-zone audit was performed in this finished-pass step. Do not confuse or synonymize it with D. carolinensis, introduced D. micrantha, D. donelliana, or nursery-marketed 'D. repens'.

best_field_traits: Creeping perennial rooting at nodes; dense low mat, leaves held above shallow/subterranean creeping stolons.
Blades round to kidney-shaped with a conspicuous basal notch, entire/wavy edges, several basal radiating palmate veins; ALTERNATE on runners.
Stems and lower leaf surfaces conspicuously tawny silky-hairy (sericeous), often more hairy underneath than on upper surface.
Single tiny pale-green to white cup/funnel flower, five corolla lobes, from an axil; look UNDER leaves, not for showy morning-glory trumpets.
CRITICAL: the upper end of the short pedicel hooks/recurves downward near the calyx. Photograph the entire attached stalk, not a fallen fruit.
Five rather broadly rounded, overlapping, persistent sepals (2.9–3.8 mm in fruit per FNA) typically shorter to barely longer than the mature 3–4 mm fruit.
Fruit a 2-lobed hairy capsule with fragile wall and separating lobes; do NOT confuse the sepals with flower petals.
morphology_keys.growth_habit: Perennial, clonal creeping mat in gravelly oak woodland, disturbed sites, lakeshore margins; often only a few centimeters high aboveground. Roots form at nodes; perennial slender stolons commonly shallow or just below soil surface.
morphology_keys.leaf_arrangement: Alternate, not opposite; one leaf per node along creeping shoot (dense nodes may give a paired appearance).
morphology_keys.leaves: Rounded/reniform blades with cordate basal notch and entire or subtly wavy margins; palmate veins 5–7 in local Williamson flora. FNA typical 20–30 mm long and 30–40 mm wide, with broad individual ranges; a local UT Williamson account measured smaller material (<5–23 x <10–30 mm). Do not require a rigid cutoff.
morphology_keys.leaf_surface: Silky tawny hairs on stems, more dense beneath the blade and on margins, sparse on upper leaf face. Inspect with hand lens; leaf hair is supporting, not exclusive, identification.
morphology_keys.petiole: Long relative to small hidden inflorescences. Flora of North America reports 20–170 mm including long extremes; UT Williamson County flora measured roughly 10–35 mm on local material.
morphology_keys.flowers: Tiny, solitary to paired axillary flowers; five broad lobes of a fused pale-green or creamy-white funnel/cup corolla, approximately 3.1–4 mm FNA (local measured examples can be smaller). Persistent, five-lobed calyx outside corolla.
morphology_keys.pedicel: FNA: 5–13 mm, conspicuously recurved near tip. UT Williamson: very short, hooked and downward-pointing, increasing toward fruit, to roughly 12 mm; photograph the full pedicel and whether the curve is immediately below flower.
morphology_keys.sepals: Five green calyx lobes, densely ciliate/soft hairy and overlapping. FNA: 2.5–3.2 mm at bloom, 2.9–3.8 mm in fruit. Compare length against mature fruit; they are shorter to only slightly longer, unlike Carolina ponyfoot's sepals longer than fruit.
morphology_keys.fruit: Two-lobed capsule with hairy developing fruit, each lobe one seeded; FNA 3–4 × 2.8–3.3 mm; fruit wall fragile, breaks irregularly, often fruit lobes separate. A mature fruit is a stronger species key than leaf color.
morphology_keys.habitat: Disturbed gravelly oak woodland and lakeshore edge, often under tree cover. Williamson County population descriptions and published Texas site flora document regional habitat; do not assume all low patches on urban turf are this species.
morphology_keys.flowering: FNA February–July in Texas. Timing depends on seasonal conditions; fruit stalk persists beyond bloom.
morphology_keys.field_caution: D. carolinensis and D. micrantha can look similar vegetatively, and D. donelliana also has a recurved stalk. Use a carefully photographed flower or mature fruit, with mm reference, for strict species discrimination.

comparisons.key_distinctions: D. carolinensis typically has straight or barely nodding fruit pedicel and sepals longer than fruits; D. recurvata has sharply recurved stalk near tip, larger mean flower/fruit and sepals shorter or barely longer than fruit. D. micrantha also has recurved pedicel but fruiting sepals only 2–2.5 mm and fruits 2–2.6 mm. D. donelliana's typical blade and pale corolla tend smaller despite also recurved pedicel. D. argentea has conspicuously silvery leaves; round dollarweed leaves have centrally attached peltate petioles and scallops. Straggler daisy has opposite toothed leaves and a yellow composite head; frogfruit has opposite leaves with a raised pale button inflorescence.

ecological_notes.habitat: Texas endemic according to Flora of North America/World Flora Online. Recorded in disturbed gravelly oak woodlands, lakeshores, and central Texas hill-country flora.
ecological_notes.restoration_relevance: Native low cover can be valued as a component of natural woodland/edge ground layer. Do not confuse nursery-sold 'Dichondra repens' or silver selections with sourced local D. recurvata.
ecological_notes.conservation_caution: Species occurrence does not imply county-specific verified native status within user's custom BONAP range, and plant-identification only does not justify a purchase/provenance decision.
ecological_notes.lepidoptera_bees: Do not invent larval host or bee association scores without linked, species-specific datasets.

family_genus_teaching.family: Convolvulaceae (morning glory family): Dichondra is a low-growing tiny-flowered relative, not a trumpet-flowered climbing Ipomoea. A small 5-lobed COROLLA and five green SEPALS surrounding the fruit anchor family anatomy.
family_genus_teaching.genus: Dichondra: alternate reniform petiolate leaves from creeping rooted runners and very small axillary flowers; separate species by complete pedicel curvature, hairy calyx and mature fruit size.
family_genus_teaching.species: D. recurvata: recurved/hooked tip of fruiting stalk, dense tawny silky hairs beneath leaf, calyx roughly matches or is shorter than bigger fruit; D. carolinensis generally has straight stalk and longer sepals.
family_genus_teaching.crew_question: Can you turn over a leaf to find tawny hairs, uncover a fruit and TRACE THE WHOLE STALK to see its hook, then compare sepals to capsule under a mm ruler?
